analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA power to regulate tobacco, restricts advertising, and penalizes makers if youth smoking doesn't fall.
analysis.headline: The House committee never voted on the bill; it died after referral to a subcommittee, with no floor action in the 106th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give the Food and Drug Administration legal authority over tobacco products, adopting rules the FDA had issued in 1996 to keep cigarettes away from children. It would ban tobacco ads on broadcast media, impose tougher warning labels, require smoke-free policies in public buildings, fund a $500 million anti-tobacco public awareness campaign, and penalize manufacturers whose products keep being used by children through mandatory price increases whose proceeds go to the Treasury. It died in committee without any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, who would face tighter limits on tobacco advertising, marketing, and access; nonsmokers and workers in public buildings, who would get legally enforceable smoke-free environments; and taxpayers generally, since tobacco-related disease is a major driver of public health costs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes the FDA's 1996 tobacco rule into law and gives the agency jurisdiction over tobacco products as drugs or devices, restoring the legal footing the Supreme Court had taken away, and requires additional restrictions on marketing, advertising, and access modeled on the 1997 state settlement [S2][S3].

It makes it unlawful to advertise tobacco products on any medium subject to FCC jurisdiction, and requires the Secretary to promulgate the stronger warning labels specified in the 1997 state settlement [S3].

Each manufacturer must cut the share of children using its products — 33% below baseline by years three and four, rising to 80% by year ten — or face escalating mandatory price increases, carton-only sales, and eventually plain black-and-white packaging, with the price-increase proceeds paid into the Treasury for enforcement and prevention [S3].
Public facilities where interstate-commerce activities occur must adopt smoke-free policies, enforceable by citizens, state agencies, or the EPA with civil penalties up to $5,000 per day [S2][S3].
The bill makes $500 million available for a national anti-tobacco awareness campaign and $300 million for federal enforcement, with amounts adjusted for inflation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers bear the cost of regulation, advertising bans, licensing, and youth-use penalties, and adult smokers would pay higher cigarette prices whenever a manufacturer misses its youth-use targets, since the required price increases are charged per unit sold.

drawbacks.text: The required price increases are passed through to all purchasers, so adult smokers — many of them lower-income — would effectively fund the penalty payments into the Treasury whenever a manufacturer misses its youth-use targets [S3].

The bill preempts states from requiring any health-related statement on tobacco packaging or advertising beyond the federal warnings, and repeals the existing Federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act, which could strip some states of stricter labeling rules they currently impose [S3].

Companies that fail to meet youth-use targets for three or more consecutive years would be forced to sell only by the carton and use plain black-and-white packaging, a blunt instrument that penalizes the company but stops short of stronger remedies like license revocation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health upside — fewer children smoking, secondhand-smoke protections, and funded enforcement — is large and well documented as the intent of the 1996 FDA rule and the 1997 settlement terms the bill adopts. The main costs fall on tobacco companies, which is the point, and partly on adult smokers through pass-through price increases. The state preemption clause is the weakest part, trading away some states' ability to set stronger warnings in exchange for a federal floor. On balance the bill is designed to shift a large, concentrated industry cost into public-health gains.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Health and Environment subcommittee, where it sat with no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the Child Tobacco Use Prevention Act of 2000 on March 21, 2000, joined by seven original cosponsors [S1][S3][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced [S5].
On March 30, 2000, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment — the last action of any kind in the record [S5].
No committee vote, House vote, or Senate action ever occurred, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and retailers, who avoided FDA regulation, broadcast advertising bans, and youth-use penalties for another decade; the public continued to bear the health costs of underage smoking.

for.name: Rep. Henry A. Waxman
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA); bill sponsor and senior member of the Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it at introduction; it was referred to his full committee but never brought up.

for.name: Reps. Meehan, Doggett, Markey, DeLauro, Stark, Slaughter, and Weygand
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 21 of 22 cosponsors House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; only one Republican signed on.

against.name: Chair Thomas J. Bliley Jr.
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration or a markup; the bill died in his committee without action.

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.what_they_did: Faced a bill imposing FDA regulation, advertising bans, and youth-use penalties; the industry had opposed FDA jurisdiction all the way to the Supreme Court, and no tobacco-state or industry-supported path to a vote developed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was nearly all Democratic — 21 of 22 cosponsors were Democrats with a single Republican — and it died in a committee controlled by Republicans without ever reaching a vote.

industries.note: The bill would give the FDA jurisdiction over tobacco, ban broadcast advertising, mandate tougher warnings, and fine manufacturers through mandatory price increases if children keep using their products. The industry's interest in blocking it ran directly against children's health, and the bill died in committee before any vote.

Retailers would face state and federal licensing, compliance inspections, and penalties, and for persistently failing manufacturers could sell only by the carton. These burdens serve the public goal of keeping tobacco from children.

The bill makes tobacco advertising unlawful on any FCC-regulated medium, cutting off a lucrative advertising category. The industry's interest in keeping the revenue ran against the public-health goal of reducing tobacco promotion.
